title: When quantum thermal states look classical
authors: Harald Putterman, Alexander Zlokapa, Jordan Cotler
abstract: At high temperature, quantum Gibbs states retain several classical features of the maximally mixed state: the absence of entanglement, the absence of magic, analyticity of the partition function, correlation decay, and algorithmic tractability. We prove new and sharp bounds showing that these features persist down to finite temperatures independent of system size, but fail at distinct inverse-temperature scales, forming a hierarchy of classical-to-quantum transitions. Our results hold for long-range Pauli interactions with bounded strength at every site. Despite such all-to-all interactions, we show that the death of entanglement occurs at constant temperature, resolving an open question of Rouze, Franca and Alhambra (STOC'25). We give a polynomial-time classical algorithm that prepares Gibbs states up to the death of entanglement transition. Notably, this is asymptotically colder than temperatures at which quantum Gibbs samplers are known to mix quickly, as well as the original separability temperature of Bakshi et al. (FOCS'24), which we improve to be tight up to constants. At asymptotically even colder temperatures, we show that the Gibbs state remains in the thermodynamic infinite-temperature phase. This leads to polynomial-time classical algorithms for estimating thermal expectations despite both entanglement and magic, and the resolution of a correlation decay conjecture of Harrow, Mehraban and Soleimanifar (STOC'20).
summary: This paper rigorously maps out a hierarchy of transitions where quantum Gibbs states lose their non-classical features (like entanglement) as temperature decreases. By analyzing long-range Pauli Hamiltonians, the authors establish distinct critical temperatures for separability and other classical limits. This work provides polynomial-time classical algorithms to estimate thermal expectations even when these quantum correlations are present.
main_problem: The paper establishes a hierarchy of 'classical-to-quantum transitions' for quantum Gibbs states as the system is cooled from high temperature.
main_result: It proves that features like entanglement death and separability persist down to finite temperatures, forming distinct transition scales independent of system size.
method: The authors use new cluster expansion techniques and randomized sampling approaches to analyze the partition function and state properties.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum systems governed by long-range Pauli Hamiltonians ($H$) with bounded local interaction strength, allowing for analysis beyond previously restricted models.
key_observables: Separability (unentangled states), Stabilizerness (stabilizer representation), Correlation Decay, and the zero-free radius of the partition function $Z(z)$.
important_parameters: The transition scales are characterized by parameters like $ eta_{	ext{sep}} = \Theta(1/(sk))$, $ eta_{	ext{stab}}$, and the infinite-temperature phase scale $\Theta(1/(s\sqrt{k}))$.
main_assumptions: The results apply to long-range Pauli Hamiltonians with locality $k$ and strength $s$, utilizing advanced cluster expansion methods.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares various physical properties (separability, phase transitions) across different temperature thresholds based on the system parameters $s, k,$ and $\epsilon$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing bounds related to the infinite-temperature phase using Lee-Yang theory, then deriving specific transition scales for separability and stabilizer structure, culminating in polynomial-time classical algorithms for thermal expectation estimation.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools to characterize when complex quantum many-body states simplify into classically describable forms at finite temperatures, which is crucial for understanding thermalization dynamics.
